pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — ocean food webs: multiple interconnected food chains where energy flows from phytoplankton (producers) through zooplankton, small fish and large predators, and removing one species affects the whole web.
• Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2): Y4 'construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey' — the web extends this to interconnected chains.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-LS2-1 (model movement of matter among producers, consumers, decomposers and the environment); 3-LS4-4 (effects when the environment changes) — the interdependence and disturbance ideas.
• Operational details: the leap from chain to WEB is that most animals eat, and are eaten by, MORE THAN ONE thing — so the diagram branches. Introduce producer/consumer vocabulary and (lightly) that energy flows upward and thins at each level. The signature reasoning move is DISTURBANCE: remove or crash one species and trace the knock-on effects along multiple paths (a cascade). Keep the arrow = 'is eaten by' / 'energy flows to' convention rigorous.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7–8): distinguishes a web (branching) from a single chain; Tier B (~8–9): traces ≥2 energy paths through a web; Tier C (~9): predicts and explains knock-on effects of removing one species along more than one path.
bestPractices: Build the web up FROM chains the child already knows: overlay two or three ocean chains that share species and let the branching structure emerge — don't present a finished tangle.
Make interdependence testable by disturbance: 'remove the small fish — now what?' and trace effects along every connected arrow (this is the web's whole payoff over a chain).
Keep arrow semantics explicit and consistent ('energy flows to / is eaten by') to prevent reversal in the more complex diagram.
Introduce producer/consumer roles and that many animals occupy multiple links (eat several prey, eaten by several predators) — the defining property of a web.
Use a real, coherent ocean web (phytoplankton–zooplankton–small fish–squid–seals–sharks) rather than mixing incompatible species.
keyRepresentations: A branching ocean web with multiple arrows in/out of key species
Overlaid transparent food chains that combine into one web (build-up view)
A disturbance/removal overlay that greys out everything a lost species fed or fed on
Producer/consumer role tags and an upward energy-flow indicator
commonMisconceptions: 'A web is just a longer chain' — missing that the defining feature is multiple, branching feeding links.
Arrow reversal — reading arrows as 'eats' rather than 'energy flows to / is eaten by', more error-prone in a dense web.
'Removing a predator only helps' — not anticipating cascades (prey booms, overgrazes, other species crash).
'Only the directly-connected animal is affected' — not tracing effects along multiple/indirect paths.
'Top predators are most important; tiny plankton don't matter' — undervaluing producers at the web's base.

learn.summary: Ocean food webs for ages 7–9: multiple interconnected food chains where energy flows from phytoplankton (producers) through zooplankton, small fish, squid, seals and sharks. The core moves are seeing that most animals eat and are eaten by MORE THAN ONE thing (so a chain becomes a branching web), tracing energy along multiple paths, and reasoning about disturbance — removing one species and following the likely knock-on effects (a cascade) along several paths, both up to predators and down to prey. Outcomes are kept qualitative ('may increase/decline') rather than guaranteed.

activities.title: Overlay chains to build a branching web, then pull one thread
feedback: If arrows get reversed in the denser diagram, re-read each as 'energy flows TO the eater' and re-point it; reversal is a common error in a crowded web.
If the child says only the removed species is affected, prompt: who ate it? (they lose that food) and what did it eat? (that may increase) — follow two or three links so the ripple becomes visible.
If the child treats removal as simply 'good' for the prey, balance the ledger: the prey may increase, but predators lose food and that spreads too — effects go in BOTH directions.
If the child reasons as one straight chain, point to a predator with several prey and ask what its backup food is: losing one prey still hurts, but the branching links share the impact.
activities.rationale: The topic's signature reasoning is interconnection and cascading disturbance. Building the web up from familiar chains (rather than presenting a finished tangle) lets the branching structure emerge, and running removals makes interdependence testable and traceable along multiple paths.
sourceClaims: UK Lower KS2 Y4 science requires pupils to construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.
NGSS 5-LS2-1 asks students to model the movement of matter among producers, consumers, decomposers and the environment, capturing interdependence in a food web.
In marine food webs most species have multiple feeding links, and removing or depleting one species (e.g. through overfishing) can trigger cascading changes across the web.
learnerActions: Start with two or three ocean food chains the child already knows (e.g. phytoplankton→zooplankton→small fish→squid→seals→sharks) and find the species they share.

Draw or drag 'energy flows to / is eaten by' arrows to join the chains where they share a species, so a single line becomes a branching WEB — notice that many animals now feed on, or are fed on by, more than one other species (though not every one: in this web sharks are not eaten by anything shown, and zooplankton eat only phytoplankton).
Check each arrow points from the eaten to the eater (energy flows to the eater); fix any reversed arrows.

Remove or crash one species (e.g. overfish the small fish) and trace the likely effects out loud along every connected arrow: predators that ate it (squid and seals) lose that food source and may decline; prey it used to eat (zooplankton) may increase; follow the ripple to indirectly connected species too (e.g. sharks that ate the squid and seals), which may also be affected.
Run two or three different removals and compare how far and in which directions each cascade may spread.
activities.intendedInsight: A food web is many food chains linked together: because most animals have multiple feeding links, removing one species can spread change along many paths at once, unlike a single straight chain where each animal has at most one link above and one below.

activities.title: Read a web: tap a species to see all its links
feedback: If the child names only one predator or one prey, point back to the diagram and ask them to trace every arrow touching that species.
If plankton are dismissed as unimportant, note that producers at the base support everything above them.
This reading view shows first-order (directly connected) effects only; to see how change may spread further, trace the links yourself along successive arrows.
activities.rationale: A pre-drawn web with highlightable links can convey branching structure at low cost and supports the 'distinguish web from chain' and 'trace a path' goals. It is a scaffold for reading structure; a static view shows first-order effects and does not by itself play out a multi-step cascade, so pair it with hands-on tracing or removal reasoning.
sourceClaims: In marine food webs most species have multiple feeding links, and removing or depleting one species (e.g. through overfishing) can trigger cascading changes across the web.
learnerActions: On a pre-drawn ocean web, select a species and identify every arrow in and out of it — list all its predators and all its prey.
Count how many feeding links the species has to show it is part of a branching web, not a single chain.
For one species, state the first-order effects if it vanished (which neighbours directly lose food or lose a predator).
Tag each species as producer or consumer and note that energy flows upward from the plankton base and thins at each level as it rises (kept light at this age).
activities.intendedInsight: A web's defining feature is that species have multiple feeding links; you can read branching structure directly even before reasoning about cascades.

activities.title: Check understanding: web vs chain, trace a path, predict a removal
feedback: For web-vs-chain, correct answers cite multiple branching links, not merely the length of the diagram.
For a removal, a full response names predators that may decline AND prey that may increase, plus at least one further knock-on — not a single one-directional effect.
If the child stops at the first link, prompt them to follow the ripple one more step.
activities.rationale: Prediction, path-tracing and structural discrimination items check the three stated evidence goals. Recognition/selection items assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction that building and running a web provides.
learnerActions: Decide whether a given diagram is a web or a single chain and justify using the branching links.
Select and trace at least two different energy paths from the plankton base up to a top predator.
Given a removal scenario (e.g. almost all of one kind of small fish is fished out), predict the likely knock-on effects along more than one path and explain them.
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding is shown by distinguishing a branching web from a chain, tracing multiple energy paths, and predicting the likely cascading effects of a removal in both directions.

activities.title: Debate a fishing decision as a marine ecologist (supplementary)
feedback: If the child traces only one direction, ask them to also follow the opposite direction (e.g. after predators, consider the prey below).
If they treat a many-prey predator the same as a single-prey one, draw out that alternative food softens the loss.
activities.rationale: Discussion exercises cascade reasoning and makes thinking audible. Tracing multiple paths precisely may be clearer when the child manipulates or draws a web, so use dialogue to supplement, not replace, the hands-on building and removal work; its relative effectiveness is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: In marine food webs most species have multiple feeding links, and removing or depleting one species (e.g. through overfishing) can trigger cascading changes across the web.
learnerActions: Take on an ecologist role responding to 'what happens if we fish out the sardines (small fish)?'
Predict the cascade out loud, naming animals that lose food, animals whose prey may increase, and any indirectly affected species.

Answer probing follow-ups: 'the small fish ate zooplankton — with the small fish gone, what happens to the zooplankton and why?'; 'why does damage spread further in a web than in a single chain?'; 'would a predator with three prey be hit as hard as one that ate only the lost prey?'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating a predicted cascade in words rehearses multi-path reasoning and can surface whether the child can contrast web with chain.

constraints: Keep arrow semantics explicit and consistent ('energy flows to / is eaten by'): arrow reversal is more error-prone in a dense web.
Build the web up from chains the child already knows rather than presenting a finished tangle, so the branching structure is understood, not just copied.

Use a real, coherent ocean web (phytoplankton, zooplankton, small fish, squid, seals, sharks) rather than mixing incompatible species; do not introduce species outside this set (e.g. seabirds) unless the whole web is redefined to include them.
Treat producer/consumer roles and upward, thinning energy flow lightly at this age; the core target is branching interconnection and disturbance reasoning.
A static reading view (tap-to-highlight links) is a scaffold: it conveys structure and first-order effects but does not play out a multi-step cascade on its own.
Recognition/selection items assess understanding but do not elicit independent construction of a web or a traced cascade.

Keep removal outcomes qualitative ('may increase/decline') and cover both directions (predators losing food and possibly declining AND prey possibly increasing) plus at least one further knock-on, not a single guaranteed happy outcome.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all three sources remain marked verified:false and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted an interactive canvas is 'the definitive way to teach' and that 3D 'adds nothing' and a static image 'can't' teach the cascade. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits: a relational food web is not spatial, so a 3D build adds cost without aiding the interconnection insight; a static view shows first-order effects; hands-on building supports multi-path tracing but its relative effectiveness is untested.

The original assessment correctAnswer named 'seabirds' and 'bigger fish' as predators of the small fish, which are not in the stated coherent species set (squid, seals, sharks); the rewrite aligns predators to the stated set for internal coherence and reframes the original seabird probe. Flagged rather than silently adopting the wider species list.

Population-dynamics outcomes of a removal (prey increasing, predators declining) are simplified for ages 7–9; real cascades depend on many ecological factors. Predictions are kept qualitative and framed as 'may increase/decline' rather than guaranteed outcomes.

probeDeeper: 'You said the seabirds lose food. What happens next to THEM, and to anything that depends on them?'
'The small fish ate tiny zooplankton. With the small fish gone, what happens to the zooplankton — and why?' (downward path)
'A single food chain vs this web — why does damage spread further in a web?'
'If a predator had three different prey and one disappeared, would it be hit as hard as a predator that ate ONLY that prey? Why?'
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree — removing the small fish ripples through the whole web. Animals that ate the small fish (bigger fish, seabirds, seals) lose food and decline; the creatures the small fish used to eat (zooplankton) may increase; and predators higher up are affected too. A food WEB is many food chains linked together — most animals eat, and are eaten by, several others — so a change in one place spreads along many paths, unlike a single straight chain where each animal has just one link above and below.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks removing one species affects only that species (or only the one animal that eats it directly)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace out loud in both directions: who eats the small fish? (they lose food) and what did the small fish eat? (it may boom). Follow two or three links so the ripple becomes visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: It only affects the small fish — nothing else changes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says nothing else changes, or names just one knock-on; effect stops at the first link

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks each animal eats only ONE food (reasons as a single chain, not a web)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw two chains that share a species and show they connect into a web — a predator with several prey has a backup; losing one food still hurts but the links branch.
errorPatterns.distractor: Each animal eats only one thing, so it's just one chain
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: describes one straight chain; can't see alternative feeding paths or branching

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes removing a species is simply 'good' for whatever it ate, with no wider downside
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance the ledger: yes the prey may increase, but predators lose food and that spreads too. Removal has effects in BOTH directions, not one happy outcome.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Focuses only on the prey booming; ignores predators starving and further knock-ons

responseLevels.gap: Says removing the small fish affects only that species; reasons as one isolated link.
responseLevels.full: Traces effects along multiple paths — predators declining AND prey increasing, plus further knock-ons — and explains a food web as interconnected chains where change spreads along many links, unlike a single chain.
responseLevels.partial: Traces one knock-on effect and knows a web has many chains, but follows only a single direction (just predators, or just prey) and can't fully contrast web with chain.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In an ocean food web, fishing boats catch almost all of one kind of small fish that many animals rely on. A child says: 'That only matters for those small fish — nothing else is really affected.' Do you agree? Trace what happens to the OTHER animals in the web, and tell me how a food web is different from a single food chain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands webs traces effects along MULTIPLE paths (both up to predators and down to prey) and contrasts web with chain. A child who thinks in single chains says only the small fish (or only its direct predator) matters. The second tier (web vs chain) exposes whether they see the branching interconnection — the whole reason removal spreads.
